teaser: The only sculpture Degas ever exhibited. Critics said it belonged in a medical museum.
review_notes:
The image shows the original wax at the National Gallery of Art (yellow bodice, real tulle), consistent with the catalog.
Height about 99 cm.
Roughly 150 wax and clay sculptures found in the studio after Degas's death in 1917: the usual figure.
Materials: pigmented beeswax over a metal armature bulked with wood, rope and old paintbrushes (from NGA technical studies); human-hair wig coated in wax; linen/cotton bodice; satin ribbon; real slippers under wax. The tutu on the wax today is a later replacement: please confirm.
Marie van Goethem: born 1865 to Belgian parents, dismissed from the Opera in 1882 for missed classes; later life unknown.
Critic comparing it to specimens for a medical or ethnographic museum; words like 'monkey' and 'Aztec' appear in 1881 reviews (Paul Mantz, Elie de Mont).
Empty glass case shown in 1880.
Paul Mellon bought the wax in 1956; gift to NGA in 1999.
Bronze sold at Christie's New York in May 2022 for about 41.6 million dollars: please confirm.

lesson.text: One. That is how many sculptures Edgar Degas showed to the public in his entire life. When he died in 1917, about 150 more were found in his studio, in wax and clay, many of them crumbling. He had kept them all to himself for decades.

The one he did show is this girl. She stands about 99 centimeters tall (39 inches), roughly two-thirds the size of a real fourteen-year-old. Paris saw her in 1881, inside a glass case, at the sixth exhibition of the group we now call the Impressionists.
Degas had announced the statue for the exhibition of 1880. Visitors that year found only the glass case, standing empty. He was not ready, and he left the case there anyway.

Her name was Marie van Goethem. Her parents were Belgian, her mother a laundress, and Marie was a pupil at the ballet school of the Paris Opera. The students were nicknamed “little rats.” They came from poor families and trained for hours a day in the hope of a wage on stage.

Degas had been painting the Opera for years: rehearsals, wings, tired dancers scratching their backs. He was interested in the work, not the fairy tale. For the statue he made drawing after drawing of Marie from every side, and a nude study in wax first.
Then he did something no respectable sculptor did. A statue for exhibition was supposed to be marble or bronze, one noble material from head to toe. See what he used instead.

lesson.title: What is she made of?
lesson.text: The figure is modeled in tinted wax. The rest came from a shop.

spots.title: Hair
spots.text: Her fringe and braid are a wig of real hair, stiffened with a coat of wax so it merges with the head. In 1881 this was the detail that unsettled people most.

spots.title: The bodice
spots.text: A real fabric bodice with tiny buttons down the front, brushed over with yellowish wax. Cloth and sculpture are fused: you cannot undress her like a doll.

spots.title: The tutu
spots.text: Actual tulle, standing out in stiff layers and fraying at the hem. It is the only part that would move if you breathed on it.

spots.title: The slippers
spots.text: Real ballet slippers hide under the wax. The foot is turned fully outward, a position drilled into pupils until the hips ached.

lesson.text: Mixing real things with modeled ones was normal for shop mannequins, church saints and wax museums. It was not normal for art. Degas brought the cheap, lifelike trick into an exhibition, and applied it to a working-class child rather than a goddess.

The reviews were brutal. Critics called her ugly, wrote that she looked like a monkey or an “Aztec,” and one suggested she belonged in a museum of medicine or anthropology rather than an art show. A few saw it differently and called her the first truly modern sculpture.

In the same room, Degas hung pastel drawings of young men on trial for murder, studying their faces. Critics read the dancer's low forehead and jutting jaw in the same spirit, as signs of a “criminal type,” a pseudo-science taken seriously then.
Forget the critics for a second and read her posture the way a dance teacher would. Chin lifted. Shoulders pulled back. One leg forward, both feet turned out. And her arms?
You can see her arms going down. Where have her hands gone?

spots.title: Behind her back
spots.text: Her arms are stretched straight behind her and her fingers are locked together out of sight. It is a resting pose between exercises, and it pushes her chest and chin forward.

lesson.text: That is the ambiguity that keeps people looking. With her eyes half shut and her chin in the air, she can seem proud, bored, exhausted or defiant. Degas did not flatter her and did not mock her. He recorded a girl holding a pose because she had been told to.
X-rays show what holds her up inside: a metal frame padded out with wood, rope and even old paintbrush handles, anything Degas had lying around the studio.

After 1881 the statue went home with him and was never shown again in his lifetime. Visitors remembered seeing it in his apartment, darkening under dust. Wax is fragile: it softens in heat and cracks in cold.

His heirs decided to save what could be saved. From about 1920 a Paris foundry cast the surviving waxes in bronze, and the dancer was cast more than two dozen times. Each bronze still wears a cloth skirt and a ribbon, so no two look quite alike today.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Eyes nearly closed, lips pressed, nose tipped up. Degas left the features slightly rough, with none of the sweetness expected of a ballerina.

spots.title: The braid
spots.text: Her plait hangs down her back, tied with a ribbon whose pale end just shows past her neck from this angle.

spots.title: Collarbones
spots.text: The wax here is thin and shiny over bone. This is the chest of an underfed child, not an idealized nude.

spots.title: The forward leg
spots.text: Lumpy and visibly worked by fingers, the wax records Degas pressing and smoothing. He was a painter teaching himself to model.

spots.title: The back foot
spots.text: Planted flat and turned out at a right angle to the other. Try standing like this for a minute to feel what the pose costs.

spots.title: The wooden base
spots.text: A plain square board, like a patch of rehearsal floor. No marble pedestal lifts her out of everyday life.

lesson.text: The wax you are looking at is the one Degas made with his own hands. The American collector Paul Mellon bought it in 1956, and it has been at the National Gallery of Art in Washington since 1999.
One of the bronze casts sold at auction in New York in 2022 for about 41.6 million dollars, a record for the artist. In 1881 nobody had offered to buy her at all.

And Marie? In 1882 the Opera dismissed her for missing too many classes. After that, the records go silent. Nobody knows what became of her, how long she lived, or whether she ever learned that her face was in museums on three continents.
Degas put real hair and real cloth on a statue of a poor ballet pupil, and showed sculpture that it could deal with ordinary, unidealized life. The shock of 1881 is the reason she matters now.

quiz.question: How many sculptures did Degas exhibit during his lifetime?
quiz.explanation: The Little Dancer was the only one he ever showed publicly.

quiz.question: What did visitors find at the 1880 exhibition?
quiz.explanation: Degas was not ready and left the case standing empty.

quiz.question: What is the original figure modeled in?
quiz.explanation: The original is wax, combined with real hair and fabric.

quiz.question: Where are the dancer's hands?
quiz.explanation: Her arms stretch behind her with the fingers locked together.

quiz.question: What happened to the model, Marie van Goethem, in 1882?
options: She was dismissed from the Opera
quiz.explanation: She was dismissed for missing classes, and then disappears from the records.

quiz.question: What do X-rays reveal inside the statue?
options: A frame padded with wood, rope and paintbrush handles
quiz.explanation: Degas built the inner frame from whatever he had in the studio.

facts.text: Critics in 1881 praised the dancer's grace and prettiness.
facts.explanation: Most called her ugly, and one said she belonged in a medical or anthropology museum.

facts.text: The bronze versions were cast after Degas's death.
facts.explanation: His heirs had the waxes cast in bronze from about 1920.
At about 99 cm, she is roughly two-thirds the size of a real girl of fourteen.
